entries.title: Make a walk easier to choose
entries.prompt: I want to go for a walk but keep postponing it.
entries.text: Choose a simple route and put on your shoes. You do not need to decide on a perfect distance first.

entries.title: Make a walk easier to choose
entries.prompt: I do not know where to walk.
entries.text: Pick somewhere familiar and safe for your circumstances. A short route you already know can reduce the decisions.

entries.title: Make a walk easier to choose
entries.prompt: I want a walk without tracking steps.
entries.text: You can walk without a number. Choose the route or time that suits you and let the movement be enough.

entries.title: Make a walk easier to choose
entries.prompt: I feel awkward walking alone.
entries.text: A familiar, comfortable route may make the start easier. You can also invite someone, without waiting for company every time.

entries.title: Make a walk easier to choose
entries.prompt: Can I walk slowly?
entries.text: Yes. Choose a pace that fits your comfort and situation. A walk does not have to become a competition.

entries.title: Make a walk easier to choose
entries.prompt: I want a little walk after lunch.
entries.text: If it suits you, choose a comfortable route and pace. The After-meal stroll routine can keep the plan simple.

entries.title: Make a walk easier to choose
entries.prompt: I do not want to turn a walk into exercise homework.
entries.text: Then leave the targets out. You can notice the surroundings and return when it feels practical.

entries.title: Make a walk easier to choose
entries.prompt: I walked to the shop instead of doing a workout.
entries.text: That was still movement in your day. You can record it without pretending it was a different kind of session.

entries.title: Make a walk easier to choose
entries.prompt: I am worried about getting distracted near traffic.
entries.text: Keep your attention on the route and surroundings. Leave the screen and any inward-focus exercise until you are safely stopped.

entries.title: Make a walk easier to choose
entries.prompt: Can you choose a walking route near me?
entries.text: I do not have a verified local route here. Use a trusted map and check the route's suitability for your circumstances.

entries.title: When the weather changes the plan
entries.prompt: It is raining and I do not want to walk.
entries.text: You can choose an indoor alternative or a shorter plan. Weather changing the activity does not erase your intention.

entries.title: When the weather changes the plan
entries.prompt: It is too hot for my usual workout.
entries.text: Adjust or postpone the session if conditions are uncomfortable. A gentler indoor option may fit better than forcing the original plan.

entries.title: When the weather changes the plan
entries.prompt: The pavement is icy.
entries.text: Choose a safer option rather than keeping the walk at any cost. An indoor movement break may be enough today.

entries.title: When the weather changes the plan
entries.prompt: It is dark before I finish work.
entries.text: Consider a well-lit familiar route, a different time, or an indoor activity. Your comfort and safety matter more than the exact plan.

entries.title: When the weather changes the plan
entries.prompt: I cannot open the windows because of the weather.
entries.text: Choose an activity that feels comfortable in the room you have. You can reduce the intensity or take a rest instead.

entries.title: When the weather changes the plan
entries.prompt: I planned a run but conditions look unsafe.
entries.text: It is reasonable to change the plan. Pick another activity or wait for safer conditions.

entries.title: When the weather changes the plan
entries.prompt: I need movement for a rainy weekend.
entries.text: Look through the no-equipment routines in Move. Choose one that suits your space and current ability.

entries.title: When the weather changes the plan
entries.prompt: I feel guilty using the weather as a reason to stay in.
entries.text: You can make a practical decision without judging it. Ask whether an indoor option fits, or whether today calls for rest.

entries.title: When the weather changes the plan
entries.prompt: Can you check the weather before my walk?
entries.text: Use a current local forecast before deciding. This recording cannot check live weather or tell you conditions are safe.

entries.title: When the weather changes the plan
entries.prompt: I want a backup plan for outdoor exercise.
entries.text: Choose one indoor option in advance. A simple backup can save you from making the whole decision again on a difficult day.

entries.title: Move in the space you have
entries.prompt: My home is too small for a workout.
entries.text: Check the space needed for each movement before starting. Choose a smaller, safe option rather than forcing the routine into a cramped area.

entries.title: Move in the space you have
entries.prompt: I have downstairs neighbours and cannot jump.
entries.text: Try the Quiet living-room cardio routine. Read each movement and adapt or skip anything unsuitable for your space.

entries.title: Move in the space you have
entries.prompt: I do not own any exercise equipment.
entries.text: Several Move routines need no equipment. Start with one that matches your experience and the room available.

entries.title: Move in the space you have
entries.prompt: The floor is cluttered.
entries.text: Clear only the safe space needed before moving. If that is not possible, choose another activity or place.

entries.title: Move in the space you have
entries.prompt: Can I use household objects as weights?
entries.text: Only use equipment that is stable and suitable for the movement. If unsure, choose a no-equipment exercise or ask for qualified guidance.

entries.title: Move in the space you have
entries.prompt: I want to exercise without disturbing anyone.
entries.text: Choose quiet, controlled movements and a practical time. You can keep the session gentle and short.

entries.title: Move in the space you have
entries.prompt: I cannot get down to the floor comfortably.
entries.text: Skip floor-based movements. Choose an accessible alternative and seek tailored guidance if you need help finding suitable exercises.

entries.title: Move in the space you have
entries.prompt: I need a routine in my living room.
entries.text: Open Move and choose No equipment or Around the house. Read the routine and check the space before beginning.

entries.title: Move in the space you have
entries.prompt: My pet keeps getting under my feet.
entries.text: Pause and make the area safe before continuing. You do not need to finish a set while avoiding an obstacle.

entries.title: Move in the space you have
entries.prompt: I want to move while the house is busy.
entries.text: Find a safe space and choose a brief activity that fits. It is also okay to wait for a less crowded moment.

entries.title: Make the gym less daunting
entries.prompt: I am nervous about going to the gym.
entries.text: Give the first visit a small purpose, such as learning the layout. You do not have to master everything on arrival.

entries.title: Make the gym less daunting
entries.prompt: I do not know how to use the machines.
entries.text: Ask a qualified member of staff to show you. It is better to learn the setup than guess under load.

entries.title: Make the gym less daunting
entries.prompt: The gym is crowded and my plan is falling apart.
entries.text: You can wait, choose a suitable alternative you know, or shorten the session. The exact order is not a test.

entries.title: Make the gym less daunting
entries.prompt: I feel like everyone is watching me.
entries.text: That feeling can be uncomfortable. Keep your attention on one familiar exercise and ask staff for support if it would help.

entries.title: Make the gym less daunting
entries.prompt: I want a simple full-body gym session.
entries.text: The Gym full body routines give a starting structure. Get instruction for unfamiliar movements and choose loads appropriate to your experience.

entries.title: Make the gym less daunting
entries.prompt: I am embarrassed to ask for help at the gym.
entries.text: Learning the equipment is a reasonable reason to ask. A short question can make your session clearer and safer.

entries.title: Make the gym less daunting
entries.prompt: I forgot my usual gym equipment.
entries.text: Choose a session that works safely with what you have. You do not need to improvise a risky replacement.

entries.title: Make the gym less daunting
entries.prompt: I want to leave after ten minutes at the gym.
entries.text: You can decide what fits today. A short visit can still help you learn what would make the next one easier.

entries.title: Make the gym less daunting
entries.prompt: I am comparing my weights with someone nearby.
entries.text: Their training is not your instruction. Choose a load you can control with the technique you have learned.

entries.title: Make the gym less daunting
entries.prompt: Can you check my lifting form through this recording?
entries.text: No. This recording cannot see your technique. Ask a qualified coach for feedback on the movement you are doing.

entries.title: Learning strength work
entries.prompt: What do sets and reps mean?
entries.text: A rep is one repetition of a movement. A set is a group of those repetitions before you rest.

entries.title: Learning strength work
entries.prompt: What does three sets of eight mean?
entries.text: It means eight repetitions, then a rest, repeated for three sets. The movement and load still need to suit you.

entries.title: Learning strength work
entries.prompt: I want to gain strength without rushing.
entries.text: Learn movements you can control, keep the effort appropriate, and build gradually. Consistency can be a gentler goal than constant increases.

entries.title: Learning strength work
entries.prompt: Do I have to lift heavy on my first day?
entries.text: No. Start with learning the movement and an appropriate level of resistance. Qualified guidance can help you choose.

entries.title: Learning strength work
entries.prompt: I keep forgetting which set I am on.
entries.text: Use a simple note or the routine's set display. You do not need to hold the whole session in memory.

entries.title: Learning strength work
entries.prompt: Can strength training include bodyweight movements?
entries.text: Yes, bodyweight movements can be part of strength work. Choose versions suitable for your current ability and comfort.

entries.title: Learning strength work
entries.prompt: I want to build muscle but need a starting point.
entries.text: Start with a manageable strength routine and regular nourishment. Personal training and nutrition advice can help tailor the plan to you.

entries.title: Learning strength work
entries.prompt: I am confused by all the exercise terminology.
entries.text: Choose one movement at a time. Learn what that movement asks of you before worrying about the rest of the vocabulary.

entries.title: Learning strength work
entries.prompt: How do I know whether an exercise suits me?
entries.text: Consider your experience, comfort and any health limits. A qualified professional can help if you are unsure about a specific movement.

entries.title: Learning strength work
entries.prompt: Should I copy a strong person's programme?
entries.text: Their programme may not fit your experience or recovery. Use your own starting point and get guidance where you need it.

entries.title: Keep an honest movement record
entries.prompt: Log my strength session.
entries.text: Open Record a strength session, then check the exercises, sets, reps and weights before saving your record.

entries.title: Keep an honest movement record
entries.prompt: I forgot to record yesterday's walk.
entries.text: You can add it with yesterday's date. Use a reasonable estimate rather than inventing exact minutes you do not remember.

entries.title: Keep an honest movement record
entries.prompt: I used different weights in different sets.
entries.text: Record the sets as accurately as the form allows. A note can preserve any detail that does not fit neatly.

entries.title: Keep an honest movement record
entries.prompt: I only completed some of the routine.
entries.text: Save the steps you actually completed. The record is useful because it is honest, not because every box is filled.

entries.title: Keep an honest movement record
entries.prompt: Can I record a stretch as movement?
entries.text: Yes. Give it a clear title and record the time you actually spent, if you want it in your history.

entries.title: Keep an honest movement record
entries.prompt: I typed the wrong weight into my workout.
entries.text: Edit the saved entry and review the units and numbers before saving the correction.

entries.title: Keep an honest movement record
entries.prompt: Do I need to estimate calories burned?
entries.text: No. A useful movement record can simply describe what you did and how long it took. No calorie estimate is required.

entries.title: Keep an honest movement record
entries.prompt: I want to see my last session for this exercise.
entries.text: Look at the previous records for the same exercise. Compare like with like, including the way you performed it.

entries.title: Keep an honest movement record
entries.prompt: My activity did not save.
entries.text: Check the saved movement list before trying again, so you do not create a duplicate. If needed, keep a temporary note.

entries.title: Keep an honest movement record
entries.prompt: Can you confirm how many workouts I did this month?
entries.text: That needs your actual saved history. Open the relevant dates; this recording cannot verify a personal total.

entries.title: Build without rushing
entries.prompt: Should I increase my weights every workout?
entries.text: Progress does not have to happen every session. Keep technique and recovery in view, and seek guidance on increases that suit you.

entries.title: Build without rushing
entries.prompt: I did the same reps as last time.
entries.text: Repeating a session can still be useful practice. Look at the longer pattern rather than demanding an improvement every time.

entries.title: Build without rushing
entries.prompt: How do I know when to make an exercise harder?
entries.text: When you are comfortable with the current version, ask a qualified coach about an appropriate next step. Avoid guessing through pain.

entries.title: Build without rushing
entries.prompt: I want to add more before I have learned the basics.
entries.text: Give the basics enough time. A movement you can control is a better starting point than a bigger number you cannot manage.

entries.title: Build without rushing
entries.prompt: My strength has not changed this week.
entries.text: A week may not tell you much. Look at consistency, context and comparable records over more time.

entries.title: Build without rushing
entries.prompt: I feel stronger but the numbers are unchanged.
entries.text: Notice what has become easier or more controlled. Progress is not only an increase in the weight on the record.

entries.title: Build without rushing
entries.prompt: Can you guarantee muscle gain in a month?
entries.text: I cannot guarantee a result or timeline. Training, nourishment, recovery and individual circumstances all affect what happens.

entries.title: Build without rushing
entries.prompt: I am tempted to double everything tomorrow.
entries.text: A sudden jump is not necessary to make progress. Choose a manageable next session and build with appropriate guidance.

entries.title: Build without rushing
entries.prompt: I want a harder option for this movement.
entries.text: Use the routine's harder option only if it fits your ability and you understand the technique. You can keep the current version.

entries.title: Build without rushing
entries.prompt: I went backwards on one exercise.
entries.text: One session can vary for many reasons. Record it honestly and look at the pattern before deciding something has gone wrong.

entries.title: Recovery belongs in the plan
entries.prompt: I feel guilty taking a rest day.
entries.text: Rest can be part of training, not a break from being committed. Let today's plan reflect how you are doing.

entries.title: Recovery belongs in the plan
entries.prompt: I am tired but do not want to lose my streak.
entries.text: A streak is not more important than your wellbeing. Choose rest or a gentler option when that is what you need.

entries.title: Recovery belongs in the plan
entries.prompt: Can I have a day without tracking movement?
entries.text: Yes. You can move or rest without recording it. The app does not need evidence for every choice.

entries.title: Recovery belongs in the plan
entries.prompt: I trained hard yesterday and feel drained.
entries.text: Consider a lighter day or rest. You do not need to repeat yesterday's effort just to feel consistent.

entries.title: Recovery belongs in the plan
entries.prompt: I want a gentle recovery activity.
entries.text: Choose a comfortable easy movement you already know, or simply rest. Recovery does not need its own demanding checklist.

entries.title: Recovery belongs in the plan
entries.prompt: I am frustrated that my body needs rest.
entries.text: You can be frustrated and still respond kindly. The next useful step may be making recovery easier, not arguing with it.

entries.title: Recovery belongs in the plan
entries.prompt: I skipped today because I was exhausted.
entries.text: That was a response to the day you had. Decide the next session when you know what capacity you have.

entries.title: Recovery belongs in the plan
entries.prompt: Can more exercise make up for poor recovery?
entries.text: Adding effort is not a substitute for recovery. Consider your rest and overall load, and get tailored advice if you are struggling.

entries.title: Recovery belongs in the plan
entries.prompt: I want to plan rest without calling it failure.
entries.text: Give rest its own place in the plan. You can describe it as recovery, or simply leave that space unfilled.

entries.title: Movement that fits your body
entries.prompt: Standing exercise is not accessible to me.
entries.text: Your movement plan should fit your body. Choose suitable seated or supported options with guidance from a qualified professional where needed.

entries.title: Movement that fits your body
entries.prompt: I use a wheelchair and want to record activity.
entries.text: You can describe the activity you actually did in your movement journal. Walking is not the only movement worth recording.

entries.title: Movement that fits your body
entries.prompt: I have a disability and generic routines do not fit.
entries.text: You do not need to force the generic routine. Personalised advice can help identify movements that suit your access needs and health.

entries.title: Movement that fits your body
entries.prompt: I need a lower-impact version.
entries.text: Check the easier option and whether it is suitable for you. You can skip the movement if neither version fits.

entries.title: Movement that fits your body
entries.prompt: I cannot follow fast exercise instructions.
entries.text: Read the next step before starting and pause whenever you need. The routine can wait for you.

entries.title: Movement that fits your body
entries.prompt: I want to repeat the instruction before moving.
entries.text: Take another look at the current step. Understanding the movement matters more than keeping up with a timer.

entries.title: Movement that fits your body
entries.prompt: My energy changes a lot from day to day.
entries.text: Plan for that variation. Keep a smaller option available and seek tailored advice if you have a condition affecting activity.

entries.title: Movement that fits your body
entries.prompt: I need support for balance.
entries.text: Choose a safe, stable setup and guidance appropriate to you. Do not attempt an unsupported movement that feels unsafe.

entries.title: Movement that fits your body
entries.prompt: I cannot perform the exercise shown.
entries.text: That is useful information, not a failure. Choose an appropriate alternative or skip it; the routine should adapt to you.

entries.title: Movement that fits your body
entries.prompt: I want movement goals that are not about steps.
entries.text: You can focus on an activity, a skill, or how manageable it feels. A step count is only one possible measure.

entries.title: Encouragement without pressure
entries.prompt: Motivate me without shouting at me.
entries.text: You do not need to attack this session. Choose one comfortable beginning, and let that be enough to get moving.

entries.title: Encouragement without pressure
entries.prompt: I do not want fitness guilt.
entries.text: Then leave guilt out of the plan. Choose movement because it fits your needs today, not because you owe a punishment.

entries.title: Encouragement without pressure
entries.prompt: Can you keep me company while I exercise?
entries.text: Bounce can stay with your activity in Daywell. Choose quiet company or a little encouragement in the activity settings.

entries.title: Encouragement without pressure
entries.prompt: I want encouragement but not constant talking.
entries.text: Choose A little encouragement or Stay quiet. The company can be there without interrupting every moment.

entries.title: Encouragement without pressure
entries.prompt: I am bored of my usual workout.
entries.text: You could change one part you understand safely, or choose a different routine. Variety does not need to mean starting from zero.

entries.title: Encouragement without pressure
entries.prompt: I am not in the mood but might try a little.
entries.text: Try a small beginning and reassess. You are allowed to decide how much fits after you start.

entries.title: Encouragement without pressure
entries.prompt: I want to enjoy movement again.
entries.text: Think of an activity you like for its own sake. Music, a familiar route, or friendly company may make the choice easier.

entries.title: Encouragement without pressure
entries.prompt: I need a gentler reason to exercise.
entries.text: You might move to feel a little more capable in everyday life. It does not have to be about changing your appearance.

entries.title: Encouragement without pressure
entries.prompt: I hate being told no excuses.
entries.text: Your circumstances are real. Let the plan account for them instead of treating every difficulty as something to overpower.

entries.title: Encouragement without pressure
entries.prompt: Say something encouraging before I start.
entries.text: Start where you are today. A controlled, manageable effort is enough; you do not have to impress anyone here.

entries.title: Company and movement
entries.prompt: I would exercise more if someone joined me.
entries.text: Try one simple invitation with a specific time. A short walk can be easier to arrange than a whole new fitness plan.

entries.title: Company and movement
entries.prompt: My friend is much fitter than I am.
entries.text: Agree on a pace and activity that work for both of you. You do not need to turn shared time into a test.

entries.title: Company and movement
entries.prompt: I am worried about slowing the group down.
entries.text: Check the group's pace and expectations before joining. Finding a suitable group is more useful than forcing yourself to keep up.

entries.title: Company and movement
entries.prompt: I want to ask someone to walk with me.
entries.text: Make the invitation easy to answer: Would you like a short walk after lunch one day this week?

entries.title: Company and movement
entries.prompt: My workout partner cancelled.
entries.text: You can choose a smaller solo option or reschedule. Their cancellation does not have to decide every part of your plan.

entries.title: Company and movement
entries.prompt: I do not enjoy group exercise.
entries.text: You can choose movement on your own terms. A solo routine is just as valid a preference.

entries.title: Company and movement
entries.prompt: I feel pressured to lift what my friend lifts.
entries.text: Choose your own load and technique. Training together does not mean your bodies or experience need identical numbers.

entries.title: Company and movement
entries.prompt: I want movement time with my family.
entries.text: Choose an activity everyone can take part in comfortably. The shared experience can matter more than a training target.

entries.title: Company and movement
entries.prompt: I am embarrassed to tell a trainer I need an easier option.
entries.text: That is useful information for a trainer. Ask for a version that fits your current ability and comfort.

entries.title: Company and movement
entries.prompt: I want accountability without being judged.
entries.text: Agree on what support you actually want, such as a friendly check-in. Make clear that rest and changed plans are allowed.

entries.title: Movement away from your routine
entries.prompt: I am travelling and have no gym.
entries.text: The no-equipment routines can give you options. Check the space and choose what feels suitable after the journey.

entries.title: Movement away from your routine
entries.prompt: I have been sitting on a train for ages.
entries.text: When it is safe and practical, change position or take a gentle movement break. Stay aware of the train and people around you.

entries.title: Movement away from your routine
entries.prompt: I am stiff after a long drive.
entries.text: Wait until you are safely parked. Then choose a comfortable change of position and gentle movement without forcing a stretch.

entries.title: Movement away from your routine
entries.prompt: I want a short hotel-room routine.
entries.text: Open Hotel room fifteen in Move and review the exercises. Adapt or skip anything that does not fit the room or your body.

entries.title: Movement away from your routine
entries.prompt: I forgot my trainers on a trip.
entries.text: Choose an activity that is safe with the footwear and surroundings you have. You do not need to improvise a risky workout.

entries.title: Movement away from your routine
entries.prompt: My holiday has disrupted my exercise routine.
entries.text: You can let the holiday have a different rhythm. Notice ordinary movement without recreating every usual workout.

entries.title: Movement away from your routine
entries.prompt: I feel drained after a long flight.
entries.text: Start with rest and comfort. You can choose gentle movement when it feels appropriate, rather than forcing the usual session.

entries.title: Movement away from your routine
entries.prompt: I need a movement break at a service station.
entries.text: Once safely parked, choose a safe place to walk or change position. Keep clear of traffic and return when you feel ready.

entries.title: Movement away from your routine
entries.prompt: I want to restart after travelling.
entries.text: Use a manageable first session and see how it feels. You do not need to make up every missed activity.

entries.title: Movement away from your routine
entries.prompt: Can you track my movement automatically while I travel?
entries.text: This MVP does not automatically track your travel activity. You can add a movement record yourself when you want one.

entries.title: Understand before increasing effort
entries.prompt: I do not understand this exercise cue.
entries.text: Pause the routine and read it again. If the movement is still unclear, get a qualified demonstration rather than guessing.

entries.title: Understand before increasing effort
entries.prompt: How fast should I do these repetitions?
entries.text: Use a controlled pace you have learned for the exercise. Speed is not a substitute for understanding the movement.

entries.title: Understand before increasing effort
entries.prompt: I keep losing count while learning the movement.
entries.text: Put technique first. A simple counter or note can help, but the number does not need to override control.

entries.title: Understand before increasing effort
entries.prompt: Can I watch a demonstration before starting?
entries.text: A clear demonstration from a qualified source can help. Daywell's text cue alone may not be enough for an unfamiliar exercise.

entries.title: Understand before increasing effort
entries.prompt: I am holding my breath while lifting and feel uncomfortable.
entries.text: Stop and reset. Ask a qualified coach about breathing and technique appropriate to that lift rather than pushing through discomfort.

entries.title: Understand before increasing effort
entries.prompt: The harder version looks exciting.
entries.text: Understand the easier version first. Choose difficulty that matches your skill, not just the version that looks impressive.

entries.title: Understand before increasing effort
entries.prompt: I do not know where my feet should go.
entries.text: That detail depends on the exercise and your body. Get a clear demonstration before adding resistance or speed.

entries.title: Understand before increasing effort
entries.prompt: I want to practise rather than chase a number.
entries.text: That is a useful intention. Keep the effort manageable and notice whether the movement feels more controlled.

entries.title: Understand before increasing effort
entries.prompt: I rushed the last set and it felt messy.
entries.text: Pause before continuing. You can reduce the demand and return to a version you can control, or end the session.

entries.title: Time a little movement
entries.prompt: Start a ten-minute walk timer.
entries.text: Review the proposed walk and duration before starting. Keep Daywell open if you want the timer and companion cues.

entries.title: Time a little movement
entries.prompt: Pause my workout timer.
entries.text: Use Pause activity or the routine's Pause button. Check the on-screen timer to confirm it has stopped.

entries.title: Time a little movement
entries.prompt: Can I resume the movement timer?
entries.text: Choose Resume activity or Continue on the routine timer. Review the remaining time before carrying on.

entries.title: Time a little movement
entries.prompt: I want Bounce to stay quiet during my workout.
entries.text: Choose Stay quiet for the activity's company level. You can keep the illustration without spoken check-ins.

entries.title: Time a little movement
entries.prompt: I finished moving before the timer ended.
entries.text: You can end the activity now. If you save a record, use what you actually did rather than the original planned duration.

entries.title: Time a little movement
entries.prompt: Will this timer continue when I lock my phone?
entries.text: The browser may pause when the phone is locked. Use your device's timer for something that must work in the background.

entries.title: Time a little movement
entries.prompt: I want a timer without encouragement.
entries.text: Use Timers or choose quiet company. You do not need motivational prompts to keep time.

entries.title: Time a little movement
entries.prompt: Can you log the workout just because the timer ended?
entries.text: A finished timer does not prove what movement happened. Review and save the activity details yourself.

entries.title: Time a little movement
entries.prompt: I accidentally started the wrong movement timer.
entries.text: End the incorrect activity, then review the right title and duration before starting again.

entries.title: Time a little movement
entries.prompt: I want to change the length of my walk.
entries.text: Check the activity controls before changing the plan. Keep the saved record separate from what you originally intended.

entries.title: Return without making up for it
entries.prompt: I missed a week of movement.
entries.text: Begin with what fits today. There is no exercise debt to repay before you are allowed to return.

entries.title: Return without making up for it
entries.prompt: I keep starting and stopping exercise plans.
entries.text: Look for the part that repeatedly becomes difficult. A smaller or more flexible plan may be easier to return to.

entries.title: Return without making up for it
entries.prompt: I was consistent and then life got busy.
entries.text: The earlier movement still happened. Adjust the next step to your current life instead of trying to recreate a different week.

entries.title: Return without making up for it
entries.prompt: I want to restart without announcing a big goal.
entries.text: You can quietly choose one session. A fresh start does not need a public promise or a complete new identity.

entries.title: Return without making up for it
entries.prompt: I missed Monday so the week feels ruined.
entries.text: The rest of the week is still available. Choose the next practical opportunity without making Monday decide everything.

entries.title: Return without making up for it
entries.prompt: I want a routine I can keep returning to.
entries.text: Choose something manageable on an ordinary day, with an even smaller version for difficult days.

entries.title: Return without making up for it
entries.prompt: I did less this month than last month.
entries.text: Look at what changed around you. A fair comparison includes time, health, responsibilities and the opportunities you actually had.

entries.title: Return without making up for it
entries.prompt: I need to restart after caring for someone.
entries.text: Caring can take real energy. Begin with a small activity that fits your current responsibilities and leaves room for your own rest.

entries.title: Return without making up for it
entries.prompt: I am afraid another attempt will not last.
entries.text: You do not need a lifetime promise to choose today. Make the next step useful even if the pattern changes later.

entries.title: Return without making up for it
entries.prompt: I want to celebrate coming back.
entries.text: Returning is worth noticing. Keep the celebration gentle and let the next session stay manageable.

entries.title: Choosing something to eat
entries.prompt: I cannot decide what to eat tonight.
entries.text: Let's make the choice smaller. Would something warm or something cold feel easier tonight?

entries.title: Choosing something to eat
entries.prompt: Nothing in the fridge appeals to me.
entries.text: Start with the easiest ingredient you have. It only needs to become a manageable meal, not an exciting one.

entries.title: Choosing something to eat
entries.prompt: I have looked at delivery menus for an hour.
entries.text: Choose one familiar place, then one meal you usually enjoy. You can stop comparing once that choice is made.

entries.title: Choosing something to eat
entries.prompt: What is a low effort dinner?
entries.text: Toast with eggs, beans, or another topping you enjoy can be a starting point. Add something fresh if it is available.

entries.title: Choosing something to eat
entries.prompt: I want dinner without lots of washing up.
entries.text: A filled wrap or a simple sandwich can keep the dishes down. Choose a filling that suits your needs.

entries.title: Choosing something to eat
entries.prompt: I need someone to narrow my food options.
entries.text: Let's choose between two: a simple pasta meal or a filled sandwich. Which sounds more manageable?

entries.title: Choosing something to eat
entries.prompt: I keep changing my mind about lunch.
entries.text: Pick something familiar that fits what you have. Lunch does not have to be the best possible choice.

entries.title: Choosing something to eat
entries.prompt: Everyone at home wants a different meal.
entries.text: Could you share one base, like rice or bread, and let people choose their own toppings?

entries.title: Choosing something to eat
entries.prompt: I am too tired to follow a recipe.
entries.text: An assembled meal counts. Put together a few ready to eat foods you like, without turning it into a cooking project.

entries.title: Choosing something to eat
entries.prompt: Can you choose a meal from what I own?
entries.text: Tell me a few ingredients you have and any dietary needs. We can then narrow the options together.

entries.title: Food when time is short
entries.prompt: I have ten minutes before my next meeting.
entries.text: Use that time for something straightforward to eat. A sandwich or leftovers may be enough to get lunch started.

entries.title: Food when time is short
entries.prompt: I need breakfast I can take with me.
entries.text: Try preparing something portable that you enjoy, such as overnight oats or a filled roll, when you have a moment.

entries.title: Food when time is short
entries.prompt: I cannot cook today.
entries.text: You can still have a meal. Ready to eat ingredients and prepared food are useful options on a day like this.

entries.title: Food when time is short
entries.prompt: I need a meal with almost no chopping.
entries.text: Frozen vegetables, tinned pulses, and ready prepared ingredients can reduce the preparation. Choose what works for your kitchen.

entries.title: Food when time is short
entries.prompt: I have only one clean bowl.
entries.text: A bowl of cereal, soup, or a simple rice meal could work. Start with food; the rest can wait.

entries.title: Food when time is short
entries.prompt: Can frozen food count as a proper meal?
entries.text: Yes. Frozen ingredients and prepared meals can be useful parts of everyday eating. Follow the preparation instructions.

entries.title: Food when time is short
entries.prompt: I need something after getting home late.
entries.text: Keep the decision gentle. A familiar, easy meal is enough tonight; it does not need extra steps.

entries.title: Food when time is short
entries.prompt: I forgot to defrost anything.
entries.text: Look for food you can use safely as it is, or cook from frozen if the label allows it. You can change the plan.

entries.title: Food when time is short
entries.prompt: My lunch break got cut short.
entries.text: See whether you can protect a few minutes to eat now, and make room for more food later if you need it.

entries.title: Food when time is short
entries.prompt: I need a backup meal for busy nights.
entries.text: Choose one shelf or freezer meal you already like. Keep its ingredients together so there is less to think about.

entries.title: Use what is already here
entries.prompt: I have pasta and a tin of tomatoes.
entries.text: That can be a simple starting point. If you have beans, lentils, or another protein you enjoy, you could add some.

entries.title: Use what is already here
entries.prompt: I have rice but no dinner plan.
entries.text: Think of rice as the base. Check for a suitable topping, some vegetables, and a sauce or seasoning you enjoy.

entries.title: Use what is already here
entries.prompt: How do I use up these vegetables?
entries.text: Tell me which vegetables you have and whether they are still fresh. We can find a simple way to use them.

entries.title: Use what is already here
entries.prompt: I keep buying ingredients I already own.
entries.text: Before your next shop, take a quick look at one cupboard and the fridge. A short list can be enough.

entries.title: Use what is already here
entries.prompt: My cupboards are full but I feel like there is no food.
entries.text: Pick one familiar meal, then check only for its ingredients. You do not need to organise every cupboard first.

entries.title: Use what is already here
entries.prompt: I want to clear a little freezer space.
entries.text: Choose one item you can safely use this week. Build a meal around that before adding anything new.

entries.title: Use what is already here
entries.prompt: Can you suggest a meal from a photo of my fridge?
entries.text: A photo may miss labels, dates, and ingredients. Tell me what is there and any food restrictions before we choose.

entries.title: Use what is already here
entries.prompt: I bought too many fresh ingredients.
entries.text: Choose one to use soon. Check reliable storage or freezing guidance for the others, so you do not have to rush through everything.

entries.title: Use what is already here
entries.prompt: I cannot remember when I opened this food.
entries.text: Check its label and reliable food safety guidance. If you cannot establish that it is safe, choose something else.

entries.title: Use what is already here
entries.prompt: Can you tell if this leftover is safe to eat?
entries.text: I cannot confirm food safety from a description alone. Storage time, temperature, and the food itself all matter.

entries.title: An easier food shop
entries.prompt: Put milk on my food list.
entries.text: Open your food shopping list to add milk. This recording cannot save the item for you.

entries.title: An easier food shop
entries.prompt: Add the ingredients for tomorrow's dinner.
entries.text: First choose the meal and check what you already have. The remaining ingredients can go on your food shopping list.

entries.title: An easier food shop
entries.prompt: What should I buy for three easy meals?
entries.text: Start with three meals you know you will eat. Reusing a few ingredients can make the list shorter.

entries.title: An easier food shop
entries.prompt: I get overwhelmed at the supermarket.
entries.text: A short list grouped by section may help. You can shop for a few days instead of solving the whole week.

entries.title: An easier food shop
entries.prompt: I keep forgetting a key ingredient.
entries.text: Write the meal name beside its ingredients. Before leaving, check the list against what you already have.

entries.title: An easier food shop
entries.prompt: Can you read my shopping list aloud?
entries.text: Your saved list needs to be opened before its items can be read. A prepared recording cannot know what is on it.

entries.title: An easier food shop
entries.prompt: Remove bread from my shopping list.
entries.text: You can remove bread in the food shopping list. Check the right item before deleting it.

entries.title: An easier food shop
entries.prompt: I need a small shop, not a huge weekly shop.
entries.text: Choose food for your next few meals and one easy backup. A shorter list is a valid plan.

entries.title: An easier food shop
entries.prompt: I buy too much when I go shopping.
entries.text: Try starting with meals you realistically expect to make. Leave room for convenience, rather than planning an ambitious week.

entries.title: An easier food shop
entries.prompt: Can you order all my groceries?
entries.text: Daywell does not place grocery orders. You can use your food list as a reference when ordering from your chosen shop.

entries.title: A flexible meal plan
entries.prompt: Meal planning feels like too much work.
entries.text: Plan just one meal ahead. You can repeat something familiar and leave the rest of the week open.

entries.title: A flexible meal plan
entries.prompt: I never stick to a weekly menu.
entries.text: Try a small set of options rather than fixed meals for every day. You can choose based on your energy.

entries.title: A flexible meal plan
entries.prompt: Can I eat the same lunch a few days in a row?
entries.text: Repeating a lunch you enjoy can simplify things. Aim for variety across your eating over time, without making each meal complicated.

entries.title: A flexible meal plan
entries.prompt: I need a meal plan that leaves room for changes.
entries.text: Include a quick backup meal and keep some ingredients flexible. A plan can support your day without controlling it.

entries.title: A flexible meal plan
entries.prompt: I am feeding people with different tastes.
entries.text: Meals with separate toppings or sides can offer choice without several completely different dinners.

entries.title: A flexible meal plan
entries.prompt: I want to prepare food ahead without spending Sunday cooking.
entries.text: Choose one useful preparation step, such as washing produce or making a portion for later. You can stop there.

entries.title: A flexible meal plan
entries.prompt: I planned five dinners but only cooked one.
entries.text: That tells you the plan asked for too much this week. Try fewer cooking nights and more easy options next time.

entries.title: A flexible meal plan
entries.prompt: I want a simple way to plan tomorrow's food.
entries.text: Think about when you will be home and when you will be out. Choose one realistic food option for each part of the day.

entries.title: A flexible meal plan
entries.prompt: My family meal plan changes every evening.
entries.text: Keep a few adaptable ingredients available if you can. The plan can be a set of possibilities rather than a promise.

entries.title: A manageable breakfast
entries.prompt: Breakfast feels like another task.
entries.text: Make it as familiar as possible. Keep an easy option where you can find it without searching.

entries.title: A manageable breakfast
entries.prompt: I leave home before I feel ready to eat.
entries.text: Could you take something with you for later? Make space for food in a way that fits your morning.

entries.title: A manageable breakfast
entries.prompt: I need a breakfast without cooking.
entries.text: Cereal, yoghurt with fruit, or a sandwich could be options, depending on what you enjoy and can eat.

entries.title: A manageable breakfast
entries.prompt: I want a warm breakfast with little effort.
entries.text: Porridge or toast with a familiar topping can be a simple option. Follow the preparation instructions for what you use.

entries.title: A manageable breakfast
entries.prompt: I forget breakfast when mornings are busy.
entries.text: Put a gentle reminder beside something you already do in the morning. Keep the food choice easy.

entries.title: A manageable breakfast
entries.prompt: I cannot face a large breakfast.
entries.text: You do not have to force a large meal. Start with something manageable, and seek advice if low appetite keeps making eating difficult.

entries.title: A manageable breakfast
entries.prompt: Can breakfast just be leftovers?
entries.text: Breakfast does not need special breakfast food. Safely stored and reheated leftovers can be an option you enjoy.

entries.title: A manageable breakfast
entries.prompt: I need breakfast ideas for a hotel room.
entries.text: Look for simple food you can store safely, or check what the hotel offers. You can keep the choice familiar.

entries.title: A manageable breakfast
entries.prompt: I have got bored of my usual breakfast.
entries.text: Change one part, such as the fruit or topping, before replacing the whole routine.

entries.title: A manageable breakfast
entries.prompt: I want to prepare tomorrow's breakfast tonight.
entries.text: Choose an option that stores safely overnight. Set out what you need so the morning has fewer steps.

entries.title: Make room for lunch
entries.prompt: I work through lunch almost every day.
entries.text: Could you protect a short break to eat today? Your work can have a pause without needing to be finished first.

entries.title: Make room for lunch
entries.prompt: I have no lunch packed.
entries.text: Look for one accessible option nearby or at home. You can solve today's lunch without fixing the whole routine.

entries.title: Make room for lunch
entries.prompt: I want a lunch that travels well.
entries.text: Choose food you can keep at a safe temperature. A suitable container and storage plan matter as much as the recipe.

entries.title: Make room for lunch
entries.prompt: I eat lunch while answering emails.
entries.text: If it is possible, close the messages for the first few bites. Give yourself one small part of the break back.

entries.title: Make room for lunch
entries.prompt: The staff room makes lunch stressful.
entries.text: Is there another suitable place where you could eat more comfortably? You can choose a quieter break when circumstances allow.

entries.title: Make room for lunch
entries.prompt: I keep reaching afternoon without eating.
entries.text: A visible lunch reminder may help interrupt the rush. Keep a practical food option ready for when the reminder appears.

entries.title: Make room for lunch
entries.prompt: I need lunch that does not need a microwave.
entries.text: A sandwich, filled wrap, or suitable cold meal could work. Make sure you can store it safely until lunchtime.

entries.title: Make room for lunch
entries.prompt: Can you remind me to take lunch tomorrow?
entries.text: Use a reminder you can verify in your calendar or alarm tool. This recording does not create a notification.

entries.title: Make room for lunch
entries.prompt: I only have leftovers for lunch.
entries.text: Leftovers can make lunch easier. Check how they were stored and follow safe reheating guidance where needed.

entries.title: Make room for lunch
entries.prompt: I feel guilty stopping work to eat.
entries.text: Eating is an ordinary need. A lunch break does not have to be earned by getting through the whole list.

entries.title: Dinner after a full day
entries.prompt: I get home and cannot start dinner.
entries.text: Sit down for a moment if you need to. Then choose the easiest available meal, with as few steps as possible.

entries.title: Dinner after a full day
entries.prompt: Cooking after work drains me.
entries.text: You can use prepared ingredients, repeat meals, or choose something ready made. Dinner does not need to become a second shift.

entries.title: Dinner after a full day
entries.prompt: I ordered takeaway again and feel bad.
entries.text: One food choice does not define how you look after yourself. Notice what made cooking difficult and plan a useful backup.

entries.title: Dinner after a full day
entries.prompt: I want dinner to feel comforting.
entries.text: Think of a familiar meal you enjoy. Comfort can come from something simple, warm, and easy to settle with.

entries.title: Dinner after a full day
entries.prompt: I am eating alone tonight.
entries.text: You can make the meal pleasant for yourself too. Choose somewhere comfortable and food that fits the evening you have.

entries.title: Dinner after a full day
entries.prompt: I have ingredients but the kitchen is a mess.
entries.text: Clear just enough space to prepare something safely. The whole kitchen does not need to be finished before you eat.

entries.title: Dinner after a full day
entries.prompt: Can you make dinner happen in three steps?
entries.text: Choose the meal, gather only its ingredients, then follow its cooking instructions. Keep tonight's choice simple.

entries.title: Dinner after a full day
entries.prompt: Dinner is going wrong and I am getting upset.
entries.text: Pause and make the kitchen safe first. You can switch to an easier meal; the original plan does not need rescuing at any cost.

entries.title: Dinner after a full day
entries.prompt: I do not want to cook a special meal just for myself.
entries.text: A small, familiar meal is enough. You are allowed convenience even when you are the only person eating.

entries.title: Dinner after a full day
entries.prompt: I want tomorrow's dinner to be easier.
entries.text: Choose the meal before tomorrow gets busy. Check its ingredients and any safe preparation you can do ahead.

entries.title: Something between meals
entries.prompt: I need an easy snack idea.
entries.text: Try something you enjoy and can eat comfortably, such as fruit, toast, or yoghurt. Check it suits your dietary needs.

entries.title: Something between meals
entries.prompt: Is it okay to have a snack?
entries.text: Snacks can be part of everyday eating. You do not need to turn having something to eat into a moral decision.

entries.title: Something between meals
entries.prompt: I need a snack for a long journey.
entries.text: Choose food that travels and stores safely. Keep it easy to reach when you are stopped somewhere safe to eat.

entries.title: Something between meals
entries.prompt: I want a snack but cannot decide which one.
entries.text: Would you prefer something crunchy or something soft? One small choice can narrow it down.

entries.title: Something between meals
entries.prompt: I get hungry while making dinner.
entries.text: You can have something to eat while dinner is being prepared. You do not have to wait until you are uncomfortable.

entries.title: Something between meals
entries.prompt: I forgot to take food on my trip.
entries.text: At your next safe opportunity, look for an accessible food option. Taking care of that need is part of the journey.

entries.title: Something between meals
entries.prompt: I need snacks I can keep at my desk.
entries.text: Look for food with suitable storage instructions and packaging. Keep a couple of options you actually like.

entries.title: Something between meals
entries.prompt: I always judge myself for evening snacks.
entries.text: Try describing what happened without blame. If food worries keep taking over, support from a qualified professional may help.

entries.title: Something between meals
entries.prompt: Can I include sweet food in my week?
entries.text: Enjoyment can be part of eating. You can think about the overall pattern without labelling a single food choice as a failure.

entries.title: Food alongside strength training
entries.prompt: What foods contain protein?
entries.text: Beans, lentils, tofu, eggs, dairy, fish, and meat are examples. Choose options that fit your preferences and dietary needs.

entries.title: Food alongside strength training
entries.prompt: Can I get protein from plant foods?
entries.text: Beans, lentils, tofu, and other plant foods can contribute protein. A varied eating pattern can help you include different nutrients.

entries.title: Food alongside strength training
entries.prompt: I want to eat well while getting stronger.
entries.text: Regular meals, enough food overall, and suitable protein sources can support training. A personalised plan depends on your needs.

entries.title: Food alongside strength training
entries.prompt: I need a simple protein option for lunch.
entries.text: You could add beans, tofu, egg, fish, or another suitable food you enjoy to a familiar lunch.

entries.title: Food alongside strength training
entries.prompt: I think I have to eat perfectly to build strength.
entries.text: A workable eating routine matters more than making every plate feel perfect. Leave room for ordinary meals and enjoyment.

entries.title: Food alongside strength training
entries.prompt: I cannot afford expensive gym food.
entries.text: You do not need food marketed for the gym. Everyday ingredients can be useful, including beans, lentils, and other affordable options.

entries.title: Finding an eating rhythm
entries.prompt: I forget to eat when I am absorbed in something.
entries.text: Try placing an eating break beside a regular part of your day. A visible reminder can help you notice the time.

entries.title: Finding an eating rhythm
entries.prompt: My eating routine disappears on busy days.
entries.text: Keep one reliable, easy food option available. The backup can support you when the usual routine does not fit.

entries.title: Finding an eating rhythm
entries.prompt: I want fewer all or nothing food rules.
entries.text: Choose one supportive habit rather than a strict list of restrictions. Make it something you can adapt when life changes.

entries.title: Finding an eating rhythm
entries.prompt: I missed a meal and now feel behind.
entries.text: You do not have to make the day perfect again. Think about your next practical opportunity to eat something.

entries.title: Finding an eating rhythm
entries.prompt: How can I remember to take food to work?
entries.text: Put a note beside your keys or bag, and prepare what you can safely in advance. Keep the reminder visible.

entries.title: Finding an eating rhythm
entries.prompt: My schedule changes every day.
entries.text: Try planning around events, like leaving home or finishing a shift, instead of relying only on fixed meal times.

entries.title: Finding an eating rhythm
entries.prompt: I want a gentle food reminder without calorie talk.
entries.text: You can use a simple reminder such as, have I made room to eat? No calorie target is needed for that prompt.

entries.title: Finding an eating rhythm
entries.prompt: Can you help me build a realistic food routine?
entries.text: Start by identifying the part of the day when eating is hardest. We can make one small change around that moment.

entries.title: A kinder relationship with food
entries.prompt: I feel like I ruined everything with one meal.
entries.text: One meal is not a verdict on you. You can continue your day without punishing yourself or trying to undo it.

entries.title: A kinder relationship with food
entries.prompt: I want to skip dinner because I ate dessert.
entries.text: Dessert does not mean you have lost permission to eat dinner. If these rules feel persistent, reach out for qualified support.

entries.title: A kinder relationship with food
entries.prompt: Can you shame me into eating better?
entries.text: I will not use shame around food. We can look for a small, practical change that respects your needs.

entries.title: A kinder relationship with food
entries.prompt: I keep comparing my plate to everyone else's.
entries.text: Other people's plates do not show their needs or their whole day. Bring the focus back to what supports your own eating.

entries.title: A kinder relationship with food
entries.prompt: Food tracking makes me anxious.
entries.text: You can step away from tracking. If anxiety around food is growing, a qualified professional can help you find a gentler approach.

entries.title: A kinder relationship with food
entries.prompt: I do not want a weight loss goal.
entries.text: You can focus on regular meals, enjoyment, and having energy for your day. A weight goal is not required.

entries.title: A kinder relationship with food
entries.prompt: I want you to call my food good or bad.
entries.text: I would rather help you describe what a meal offers and what you enjoy. Moral labels can make eating feel harder.

entries.title: Food within your budget
entries.prompt: Healthy food feels too expensive.
entries.text: Start with affordable foods you already use. Tinned and frozen options can help you build meals without needing speciality products.

entries.title: Food within your budget
entries.prompt: I need to spend less on lunches.
entries.text: Choose one lunch you could bring from home this week. Repeating an easy option can reduce both cost and decisions.

entries.title: Food within your budget
entries.prompt: Can you plan food around a small budget?
entries.text: Tell me your budget, what food you already have, and where you shop. Prices vary, so we would need to check the actual costs.

entries.title: Food within your budget
entries.prompt: I keep wasting expensive ingredients.
entries.text: Buy for fewer planned meals at a time if you can. Choose ingredients that work in more than one familiar dish.

entries.title: Food within your budget
entries.prompt: Do I need organic ingredients to eat well?
entries.text: You do not need to make organic food a requirement. Work with food that is accessible, affordable, and suitable for you.

entries.title: Food within your budget
entries.prompt: I want a cheap meal with beans.
entries.text: Beans can go into a jacket potato, a wrap, or a simple tomato sauce. Use the preparation directions on the label.

entries.title: Food within your budget
entries.prompt: Cooking from scratch is not always cheaper for me.
entries.text: Your time, equipment, and energy matter too. Choose the combination of prepared and homemade food that works in your circumstances.

entries.title: Food within your budget
entries.prompt: I cannot buy every ingredient in this recipe.
entries.text: Choose a simpler recipe or check which substitutions are suitable. A shorter ingredient list may fit your budget better.

entries.title: Food within your budget
entries.prompt: I do not have enough money for food this week.
entries.text: You deserve help with that. A local council, food support organisation, or trusted community service may be able to connect you with food.

entries.title: Food within your budget
entries.prompt: Can you compare prices at my local shops?
entries.text: Current prices need a live check. A saved recording cannot compare today's offers, but your shopping list can help organise the comparison.

entries.title: Keep a useful food note
entries.prompt: Log the sandwich I just ate.
entries.text: Open the food log and add the sandwich there. Check the saved entry so your record reflects what you intended.

entries.title: Keep a useful food note
entries.prompt: Show me what I ate yesterday.
entries.text: Your food history needs to be opened to answer that. A prerecorded reply cannot see yesterday's entries.

entries.title: Keep a useful food note
entries.prompt: Can you calculate calories from this photo exactly?
entries.text: A photo cannot provide an exact calorie count. Portions, ingredients, and preparation can be unclear, so estimates should be treated as uncertain.

entries.title: Keep a useful food note
entries.prompt: I forgot to log a meal.
entries.text: You can add a note later if it is useful. Your record does not need to be complete to offer something helpful.

entries.title: Keep a useful food note
entries.prompt: I only want to record whether I ate regularly.
entries.text: A simple note about meals can be enough. You do not need to record every ingredient or calorie for that purpose.

entries.title: Keep a useful food note
entries.prompt: Delete an incorrect food entry.
entries.text: Find the entry in your food history and check its details before removing it. This audio does not delete saved data.

entries.title: Keep a useful food note
entries.prompt: I want to remember a meal I enjoyed.
entries.text: Write its name and the part you liked. That can become a useful option when choosing a future meal.

entries.title: Keep a useful food note
entries.prompt: Is my food history private?
entries.text: Check Daywell's current privacy information and settings before adding sensitive details. Only share what you are comfortable recording.

entries.title: Keep a useful food note
entries.prompt: Can you see whether my eating has improved?
entries.text: That would need your actual records and a clear idea of what improvement means to you. A saved reply cannot assess the pattern.

entries.title: Keep a useful food note
entries.prompt: I do not want meal logging to become a chore.
entries.text: Keep only the details that help you. You can pause logging when it stops feeling useful.

entries.title: When starting is the hard part
entries.prompt: I know what to do but cannot start.
entries.text: Make the first action smaller than the task. Opening the document or finding one item can be the whole beginning.

entries.title: When starting is the hard part
entries.prompt: I have been staring at a blank document.
entries.text: Write one rough sentence about what the document needs to do. It can be a note to yourself, not the finished opening.

entries.title: When starting is the hard part
entries.prompt: I need to start an email I am avoiding.
entries.text: Begin with the recipient and a plain subject line. Then write the main point in words you can edit later.

entries.title: When starting is the hard part
entries.prompt: I cannot get myself away from the sofa.
entries.text: Choose one small transition that feels possible, such as putting your feet on the floor. You can decide the next step after that.

entries.title: When starting is the hard part
entries.prompt: My task feels too big to even look at.
entries.text: Name only the next visible action. You do not need to hold the whole project in mind to take that step.

entries.title: When starting is the hard part
entries.prompt: Can you sit with me while I start?
entries.text: You can use a short focus timer for company. Pick one tiny action to try while it runs, with no need to impress anyone.

entries.title: When starting is the hard part
entries.prompt: I need to tidy but do not know where to begin.
entries.text: Choose one small surface or one kind of item. Stop before the task spreads to the whole room.

entries.title: When starting is the hard part
entries.prompt: I have wasted the morning and cannot begin now.
entries.text: The next few minutes are still available. Choose a small action that fits the time you have now.

entries.title: When starting is the hard part
entries.prompt: I need a tiny first step for studying.
entries.text: Open the material and find the section you need. That is enough for the first step; reading can come next.

entries.title: When starting is the hard part
entries.prompt: Please make starting feel less serious.
entries.text: Try a small experiment: give the task two minutes of imperfect attention. You can reassess when those minutes are over.

entries.title: Choose one priority
entries.prompt: Everything on my list feels urgent.
entries.text: Check which task has a real deadline or consequence today. Start there, and let the rest wait on the list.

entries.title: Choose one priority
entries.prompt: I have too many priorities.
entries.text: Choose one thing that would make today more manageable. You can keep the other priorities visible without doing them together.

entries.title: Choose one priority
entries.prompt: Can you choose my next task from my list?
entries.text: That needs your actual task list and deadlines. Open the list so you can compare what matters most today.

entries.title: Choose one priority
entries.prompt: I keep doing easy tasks instead of the important one.
entries.text: Give the important task a very small opening, such as gathering its materials. You do not need to finish it in one go.

entries.title: Choose one priority
entries.prompt: How do I know what can wait?
entries.text: Look for a real deadline, someone depending on it, or a practical consequence. Tasks without those may have more room.

entries.title: Choose one priority
entries.prompt: I want to finish ten things this evening.
entries.text: Check how much time and energy the evening actually has. Choose a smaller set and leave some room to rest.

entries.title: Choose one priority
entries.prompt: My list is longer than the day.
entries.text: The list can hold possibilities rather than demands. Pick what realistically fits today and move the rest out of view.

entries.title: Choose one priority
entries.prompt: Someone added another urgent task.
entries.text: Before adding it, check what would need to move. You can ask which existing task should take lower priority.

entries.title: Choose one priority
entries.prompt: I cannot choose between two tasks.
entries.text: Compare their deadlines and what each one would unblock. If they are genuinely equal, choose the easier starting point.

entries.title: Choose one priority
entries.prompt: Can you set my main priority for today?
entries.text: Choose the task you want to prioritise and save it in the app. This recording cannot update the priority itself.

entries.title: Returning after distraction
entries.prompt: I opened my phone without noticing.
entries.text: You noticed now. Put it somewhere a little less convenient, then return to one small part of what you were doing.

entries.title: Returning after distraction
entries.prompt: I keep switching between browser tabs.
entries.text: Choose the one tab needed for the next step. Save the others for later if you are worried about losing them.

entries.title: Returning after distraction
entries.prompt: I got distracted five times already.
entries.text: You can return five times too. Each return is a new chance to make the task smaller or the environment easier.

entries.title: Returning after distraction
entries.prompt: My thoughts keep pulling me into other tasks.
entries.text: Keep a small place to park those tasks. Write a few words, then come back to the action in front of you.

entries.title: Returning after distraction
entries.prompt: I keep checking whether anyone has messaged me.
entries.text: If your responsibilities allow it, choose a later check in time. Close the messages for one short focus period.

entries.title: Returning after distraction
entries.prompt: The room is too noisy to concentrate.
entries.text: Could you change location, reduce one sound, or choose a task that needs less concentration for now?

entries.title: Returning after distraction
entries.prompt: I am distracted by everything on my desk.
entries.text: Move just the things that compete with the next task. You do not need a perfectly tidy desk to continue.

entries.title: Returning after distraction
entries.prompt: I lost my place after scrolling.
entries.text: Look for the last small thing you completed. Write a brief note about the next action, then begin there.

entries.title: Returning after distraction
entries.prompt: Can you block all distracting apps for me?
entries.text: Daywell does not automatically block other apps. Your device may have focus or screen time settings you can choose to use.

entries.title: Returning after distraction
entries.prompt: Remind me that I can come back after distraction.
entries.text: A distraction does not cancel the work you have done. Take one gentle return to the next visible step.

entries.title: Make the task smaller
entries.prompt: Help me break down cleaning my room.
entries.text: Choose one category first, such as clothes. Put those in their places before deciding whether to take on anything else.

entries.title: Make the task smaller
entries.prompt: How do I break down writing a report?
entries.text: List the headings, put rough notes beneath them, then work on one section. Editing can be a separate pass.

entries.title: Make the task smaller
entries.prompt: I need to prepare for an appointment.
entries.text: Find the time and location, then gather what you need to bring. Add any questions you want to remember.

entries.title: Make the task smaller
entries.prompt: Packing for my trip feels overwhelming.
entries.text: Start with the essentials you cannot easily replace. Then choose clothing for the actual days and activities ahead.

entries.title: Make the task smaller
entries.prompt: I need to make a difficult phone call.
entries.text: Write why you are calling and one sentence to open with. Keep any details you might need beside you.

entries.title: Make the task smaller
entries.prompt: My project has too many moving parts.
entries.text: List the next action for each part, then choose one that unblocks something else. You can leave the full plan on paper.

entries.title: Make the task smaller
entries.prompt: I do not know what done means for this task.
entries.text: Describe a clear stopping point in one sentence. Aim for that version before adding extra work.

entries.title: Make the task smaller
entries.prompt: Can you turn this whole project into saved tasks?
entries.text: That needs the project details and a confirmed task list. Review the steps before saving them in your planning tools.

entries.title: Make the task smaller
entries.prompt: I keep making the task bigger as I do it.
entries.text: Keep a separate note for extra ideas. Return to the stopping point you originally chose.

entries.title: Make the task smaller
entries.prompt: What is the next step after opening the document?
entries.text: Read the heading or last note, then write one rough point. Keep the next action concrete and small.

entries.title: Use time gently
entries.prompt: Start a five minute focus timer.
entries.text: Open the focus timer, choose five minutes, and press start. Check that it is running before beginning.

entries.title: Use time gently
entries.prompt: Pause my focus session.
entries.text: Use the pause control on your current timer. This prepared reply cannot pause a running session for you.

entries.title: Use time gently
entries.prompt: How much time is left on my timer?
entries.text: The remaining time needs to be read from the active timer. Open it to check the current countdown.

entries.title: Use time gently
entries.prompt: I want a shorter focus session than usual.
entries.text: Choose a duration that fits your energy today. A short session can still create a useful beginning.

entries.title: Use time gently
entries.prompt: The timer makes me feel rushed.
entries.text: You can work without a countdown or choose a gentler stopping point. The tool should support you, not add pressure.

entries.title: Use time gently
entries.prompt: Can I stop before the timer ends?
entries.text: Yes. You can stop when you need to and record what helped. Finishing a countdown is not a test of your worth.

entries.title: Use time gently
entries.prompt: Restart the timer from the beginning.
entries.text: Use the reset control and confirm the duration before starting again. Make sure you intend to clear the current countdown.

entries.title: Use time gently
entries.prompt: I finished my task before the timer.
entries.text: You can end the session there. Take a small pause before deciding whether another task belongs in this block.

entries.title: Use time gently
entries.prompt: The timer ended but I am in a good flow.
entries.text: You can choose a little more time, while checking your other needs and commitments. The timer is a guide.

entries.title: Use time gently
entries.prompt: Can you promise the timer alarm will wake me?
entries.text: Do not rely on an in app timer as a guaranteed wake up alarm. Use and test a suitable device alarm for that.

entries.title: Handle an interruption
entries.prompt: Someone interrupted me and now I cannot restart.
entries.text: Write the next small action you remember. If that is unclear, review the last thing you completed and start from there.

entries.title: Handle an interruption
entries.prompt: I need to stop working suddenly.
entries.text: Leave a brief note saying where you are and what comes next. That can make returning less demanding.

entries.title: Handle an interruption
entries.prompt: I am being interrupted every few minutes.
entries.text: Could you ask for one short protected period, or switch to work that tolerates interruptions for now?

entries.title: Handle an interruption
entries.prompt: I forgot what I was doing before the doorbell.
entries.text: Take a moment to look at your workspace. The open material or last note may show the next step.

entries.title: Handle an interruption
entries.prompt: I get angry when my focus is broken.
entries.text: Pause before responding if you can. Then explain the practical thing you need, such as a few minutes to finish a step.

entries.title: Handle an interruption
entries.prompt: I need a phrase to protect my focus time.
entries.text: You could say, I am finishing one thing; can I come back to you in a few minutes?

entries.title: Handle an interruption
entries.prompt: My day is full of unpredictable caring duties.
entries.text: Choose tasks that can be left safely at a clear stopping point. Your plan needs room for the responsibilities you have.

entries.title: Handle an interruption
entries.prompt: Can you save where I got to?
entries.text: Add a short note in the relevant task or journal entry, then check it saved. A recording cannot store that note itself.

entries.title: Handle an interruption
entries.prompt: I cannot remember the idea I had before being interrupted.
entries.text: Write any small part you still remember. If it does not return now, you can leave space and come back later.

entries.title: Handle an interruption
entries.prompt: I need to return to work after a long break.
entries.text: Start with a brief review of what is still relevant. Choose one current action instead of trying to catch up on everything.

entries.title: Move between parts of the day
entries.prompt: I cannot switch from work mode to home mode.
entries.text: Close one work item and leave a note for tomorrow. Then choose a small physical change, like putting your bag away.

entries.title: Move between parts of the day
entries.prompt: I keep working even when I meant to stop.
entries.text: Choose a clear stopping action now. Save the work, note the next step, and close the tool if your responsibilities allow it.

entries.title: Move between parts of the day
entries.prompt: I find it hard to move from one task to another.
entries.text: Give the first task a small ending. Then name only the first action of the next one.

entries.title: Move between parts of the day
entries.prompt: I have ten minutes between appointments.
entries.text: You can use that gap to settle, prepare, or simply pause. It does not need to become another work session.

entries.title: Move between parts of the day
entries.prompt: I get stuck after finishing something.
entries.text: Let there be a short pause. Then choose from a small set: rest, an ordinary need, or the next priority.

entries.title: Move between parts of the day
entries.prompt: I need to leave the house but keep adding tasks.
entries.text: Return to the essentials for leaving. Extra tasks can go on a note instead of coming with you into this moment.

entries.title: Move between parts of the day
entries.prompt: How do I end a study session without losing my place?
entries.text: Write the next question or page to return to. Leave a clear starting point for your next session.

entries.title: Move between parts of the day
entries.prompt: I want a small ritual before focusing.
entries.text: Clear a little space, choose one task, and decide a stopping point. Keep the ritual short enough to be useful.

entries.title: Move between parts of the day
entries.prompt: My commute ended but my brain is still rushing.
entries.text: Let arriving be a separate moment. Put down what you are carrying and notice that the journey has finished.

entries.title: Move between parts of the day
entries.prompt: Can you help me close the working day?
entries.text: Note anything that genuinely needs carrying forward. Then choose one sign that work is finished for now.

entries.title: Make room for imperfect work
entries.prompt: I cannot submit this because it is not perfect.
entries.text: Check it against the actual requirements. If those are met, choose one final review rather than an endless search for certainty.

entries.title: Make room for imperfect work
entries.prompt: I keep rewriting the first sentence.
entries.text: Leave a rough opening and move to the next point. The beginning may be easier to edit once the rest exists.

entries.title: Make room for imperfect work
entries.prompt: I am afraid of making a mistake.
entries.text: Look for a small, reversible next step. You can build in a check without needing certainty before every action.

entries.title: Make room for imperfect work
entries.prompt: I cannot work unless my setup is perfect.
entries.text: Choose the minimum setup the task needs. Let the first small action happen before making more improvements.

entries.title: Make room for imperfect work
entries.prompt: I compare my work to everyone else's.
entries.text: Return to what this task needs from you today. Other people's finished work does not show their drafts.

entries.title: Make room for imperfect work
entries.prompt: I spent more time planning than doing.
entries.text: Keep the plan you have and test one small step. What happens next can inform the next part of the plan.

entries.title: Make room for imperfect work
entries.prompt: I need permission to make a rough draft.
entries.text: A rough draft is a useful stage of work. Its job is to give you something to shape, not to impress.

entries.title: Make room for imperfect work
entries.prompt: I have redone this task three times.
entries.text: Check what still needs changing against a clear standard. If it meets the need, consider calling that version complete.

entries.title: Make room for imperfect work
entries.prompt: Can you guarantee my work is good enough?
